scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable. The person is a 21-year-old woman who's refusing to lend her brother her vacation money. Let me break this down step by step.

First, the situation: She and her 30-year-old brother live with their parents. He's back in school after a bad job and has been living with them for 1.5 years. She's in her third year of university, working to pay for it, and saving for a post-graduation vacation. She's managed to save $2800 so far. Her brother hasn't been on a vacation in a long time and is hinting that he needs one. Their parents suggested he could save up like she did, but he's come to her asking to borrow her money for a trip to Japan this summer or fall. She refused because she's worried he can't pay it back, given his history of being bad with money. He's upset, saying it's unfair because she's the youngest and got more opportunities, while he had to work or go to college earlier. He also thinks she's been spoiled by their parents, which she disagrees with, saying she learned to budget from her father and classes.

So, the question is: Is it morally acceptable for her to refuse to lend her brother the money?

I need to consider the moral aspects here. Let's think about the factors involved.

1. **Financial Responsibility**: She's been saving for her future vacation, which is a goal she's worked towards. She's in university, working, and managing her finances. Her brother, on the other hand, has a history of being bad with money. He makes about the same as her but is always broke. She's worried he won't be able to pay her back, which is a valid concern.

2. **Family Dynamics**: They live with their parents, who are helping her brother financially. The parents suggested he could start saving now, but he's come to her instead. Her brother feels it's unfair that she's had more opportunities, like more family trips when she was younger, while he had to work or go to college earlier. He also feels she's been spoiled, which she disputes.

3. **Moral Obligations**: Is she morally obligated to help her brother? Family support is a common value, but it's also important to consider boundaries and personal financial goals. She's already contributing by not paying rent, which allows her to save. Her brother isn't paying rent either, but he's not contributing to his own savings.

4. **Fairness and Equality**: Her brother feels it's unfair that she's had more support and opportunities. However, she's managed her money responsibly, while he hasn't. She's working towards her goals, and he's asking her to give up hers for his.

5. **Potential Consequences**: If she lends him the money and he can't pay it back, it could strain their relationship further. She might lose her savings, which is a significant amount for her. Alternatively, if she refuses, he's already upset, but she's maintaining her financial independence.

Considering all these points, it seems that her refusal is morally acceptable. She's being responsible with her money, considering her brother's history of poor financial management. She's also maintaining her own goals and independence, which are important for her future. While family support is valued, it's also crucial to set boundaries to protect oneself financially and emotionally.
